rv.q: Staff Meal feels like a portal: We tumble through its funny, eerie evocation of the moment that made—is still making—our present, and we come out the other side feeling, for all its ebb toward emptiness, full.
The play’s narrative components — a meet-cute, a culinary cult of personality — are familiar parts soldered together with an inventiveness that doesn’t hold.
The prep and plating of Staff Meal is impeccable.
Playwrights Horizons has given us some of the most striking theater this season.
For those with an open mind and heart to new WTF experiences, you might find something delectable in this play.

To be sure, Staff Meal has plenty of problems, including a lack of cohesion and a second half that is too vague to support its dark intentions, but it's always interesting when an artist adds fresh colors to his palette.
There’s enough great material in Staff Meal to furnish a half-dozen plays.
Staff Meal keeps endeavoring to keep us off balance, and succeeds all too well.
But everyone’s efforts can’t make up for the show’s directionlessness.
Staff Meal promises a nine-course tasting menu of strange theatrical flavors, but it turns out to be mostly kale.
You will be well taken care of in the hands of an exceptional cast, in a play that never forgets that its a play, grateful for you its audience, and fully present in its presentation.
Staff Meal offers a taste of the sublime, but ultimately feels unsatisfying.

Berry's unexpected monologue jolts to life a play that may be a deliberate parody of pretentious modern theater pieces, rooted in interesting but familiar ideas but weighed down by generic dialogue that drags on far too long.

It’s a funny and frightening satire about attempting to make connection and build community even when the planet might be in a doom-spiral, about humans needing nourishment by being with others, in coffee shops, restaurants, or a theater.

cn.t: Koogler's surreal, shape-shifting comedy divides critics with its intentionally puzzling structure and apocalyptic turn. Some praise its quirky humor and emotional depth, while others find it too opaque and unsatisfying despite its unpredictability.
